questions.problem:
A particle of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. The spring constant associated with the spring is $k=18\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.$ 
An external force $F(t)=12{t}^{3}\,\text{N}$ is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping, what is the governing equation?
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and  external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m,$ $k$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
4{y}^{″}=-18y+12{t}^{3}.
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+4.5y=3{t}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem:
A particle of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. The spring constant associated with the spring is $k=12\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.$  The particle is also subject to the resistive force that's proportional to the particle's velocity with a damping coefficient $c=9\,\text{kg/s},$ and an external force given by $F(t)=15\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{N}.$   

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds.  If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion, what is the governing equation?
questions.worked_solution:
The general equation of forced harmonic motion with damping is

$$
m{y}^{″}=-c{y}^{′}-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m,$ $k,$ $c$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
3{y}^{″}=-9{y}^{′}-12y+15\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}+4y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

questions.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=17{e}^{t},
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $\pi $ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=16\,⟹\,\omega =4.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is an exponential force. The constant factor in the exponent is $1,$ which is not a root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular exponential solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{t},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant to be determined.

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)={e}^{t},
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t+{e}^{t}.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

Solving with these conditions for $A$ and $B$ gives

$$
A=-1,\,B=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡4t-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t+{e}^{t}.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\pi $ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\pi .$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\pi -\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi +{e}^{\pi } \\  & =({e}^{\pi }-1)\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in centimeters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+36y=18t,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with velocity $1\,\text{cm/s},$ find the position of the particle after $2$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=36\,⟹\,\omega =6.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡6t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡6t.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is a linear polynomial. Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a linear polynomial, i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha +\beta t,
$$

where $\alpha ,\beta $ are constants to be determined.

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =0,\beta =\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{t}{2},
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡6t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡6t+\frac{t}{2}.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with velocity $1\,\text{cm/s}$, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=1.$

Solving with these conditions for $A$ and $B$ gives

$$
A=0,\,B=\frac{1}{12}
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡6t}{12}+\frac{t}{2}.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $2$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡6(2)}{12}+\frac{(2)}{2} \\  & =(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡12}{12}+1)\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+25y=24\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(25t+ϕ)+12\operatorname{sin}⁡t$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ)+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡5t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡5t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to this equation is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

First, we find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(t),$ which is the solution to the simple harmonic motion equation ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.$ It can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=25\,⟹\,\omega =5.
$$

Thus, we have:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡5t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡5t$

Next, we find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t).$ The particular solution is of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =1$ and $\beta =0.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t+ϕ)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t+ϕ)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡5t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡5t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t$

Only III matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".
